 Floods Floods and severe weather beset parts of the U.S. on Election Day
 The weather’s effect on voter turnout will be watched closely by campaigns seeking to draw as many supporters out to the polls as possible. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 
 Election Day weather: 'TODAY’s' Al Roker tracks the forecast 01:07 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 3, 2026, 5:54 AM EST  /  Updated   Nov. 3, 2026, 1:40 PM EST By Evan Bush and Adela Suliman Flash flooding, heavy rain and tornadoes have forced election officials in three different regions across the United States to move polling locations, scrambling Election Day plans in hot-button races. 
 At least 21 polling locations were moved across eight Florida counties — including Brevard, Broward, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties — after intense rain caused flash floods Monday and into Tuesday morning.
 Roads were impassable in several parts of the state’s Atlantic coast after a storm dumped as much as 22 inches of rain in 24 hours in a storm that “ exceeded everyone’s expectations ,” as one forecaster put it. 
 Severe storms were moving across Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas overnight. Forecasters issued a tornado watch that lasted until about 2:45 a.m. local time Tuesday . 
 Palm Bay, Florida, gets nearly 20 inches of rain in 1 day 00:30 Forecasters were also predicting possible flash flooding in parts of Alabama, Tennessee, Arkansas and Mississippi on Tuesday, as that storm system continued to travel east . A flood watch remained in effect in some parts of Florida, though rainfall rates were slowing. 
 “Areas affected by catastrophic flooding remain extremely sensitive to any additional rainfall,” forecasters wrote in a Tuesday morning discussion . 
 In Oklahoma, a tornado Sunday forced Cimarron County officials to change one of its polling locations . The tornado, which had peak winds of about 100 mph, snapped tree branches, damaged the roof of the Keyes Community Center and collapsed a wall, according to a damage survey report from the National Weather Service . 
 Follow live updates on the midterm elections 
 In an emergency request, county election officials said the tornado caused “ considerable structural damage ” to the community center “rendering the polling location unsafe.” 
 And after historic flooding in the Four Corners region, Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre M. Henderson declared a state of emergency and issued a special accommodation that will allow voters registered in San Juan County who are isolated by floodwaters to request and return ballots electronically.
 Utah issues emergency elections order after flooding 01:06 The Colorado secretary of state is allowing a similar measure for voters — allowing votes online — in La Plata and Archuleta counties, according to 9 News . 
 In Florida, Port St. Lucie resident Jessica Rendon said she spent hours trying to cast her ballot after the weekend’s severe flooding led to waterlogged highways and closed polling locations.
 “I personally did not see one officer out in public helping any of us out,” Rendon said. “Voting or not voting.”
 She said she learned that her polling location had changed only from another resident who was also out trying to vote. Other residents who have located their polling stations are sharing the information via social media. 
 “Unfortunately, many by me are still stuck in their homes,” Rendon said, noting that the only reason she is been able to get around is that she owns a truck. “Frankly, I don’t think a lot can vote because of this.” 
 An overturned mobile home and other debris in the Verde River as severe flooding rushed through an RV park in Camp Verde, Ariz., on Monday. Ross D. Franklin / AP More Election Day surprises could be in store.
 Experts say inclement weather has suppressed voter turnout in past elections . In research of elections from 1948 to 2000, researchers observed a modest drop in turnout during unusually intense rainstorms. 
 “What we found was that for every inch of rain that a county received above its average amount of rainfall, voter turnout went down about eight-tenths of 1 percentage point,” said Brad Gomez, an associate professor of political science at Florida State University.

 Slide 1 of 1 But experts said the effect of rain on turnout is diminishing over time as more people choose to vote early or vote by mail, and they said it’s hard to predict what effect the inclement weather will have, if any, on key races. 
 In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in seven counties along the Atlantic Seaboard that are being hit with flash flooding and extreme precipitation.
 Damage in parts of Colorado remains widespread after heavy rain and flooding, with first responders searching for people who may be stranded across the area, including by helicopter.
 A vehicle bobs on the Piedras River in Arboles, Colo., on Monday. Gregory Bull / AP People with homes along the Animas River in southwestern Colorado were also facing evacuation. 
 Record rainfall was also reported in usually dry Arizona, causing deadly flooding and power outages. 
 The brief closure of two voting centers in Maricopa County sparked a chorus of conspiracy insinuations online Monday. Two out of the 254 polling locations in the county had to be temporarily shuttered “due to power related issues,” election authorities announced on social media.
 The two polling locations have since been reopened, authorities said, but some online used the shutdown to allege impropriety in the competitive swing state.
 Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs issued a statewide emergency declaration Monday after recently issuing an emergency for Navajo and Coconino counties. The governors of New Mexico and Colorado also asked President Donald Trump to declare a major disaster to receive federal funding assistance.
 Mobile homes, cottages and vehicles are strewn along the Verde River in Camp Verde, Ariz., on Monday. Ross D. Franklin / AP Rain is also expected to hit the central U.S. as voters head to the polls there Tuesday, but experts said the impact on the election outcome is expected to be minimal. 
 The weather’s effect on voter turnout will be watched closely by campaigns seeking to draw as many supporters as possible to polling places. 
 The storm system will move east Tuesday, with heavy rain possible in Mississippi, Missouri and western Tennessee.
 Man records rescue after truck gets stuck in raging floodwaters in Arizona 00:44 On Election Day, “scattered flash floods are possible” in the lower Mississippi River valley and into areas such as Memphis, Tennessee, said Jennifer Tate, a meteorologist with the weather service’s Weather Prediction Center in College Park, Maryland.
 Much of the rest of the central U.S. — from east Texas to the Midwest — can expect wet, dreary weather on Election Day.
 Election Day weather on the West Coast looks mostly pleasant, with pockets of rain in Northern California. Outside of Florida, the East Coast looks clear, though some rain is expected in Maine.
